author: Sedhu Madhavan S
headline: Specialist Data Engineer @LTM | Databricks Solutions Architect Champion🏆! 6× Microsoft Certified | Building Scalable Pipelines with Databricks, Snowflake & PySpark | AI/ML-Ready Data Solutions
text:
Stop mixing up CDC, CDF, and SCD Type 2! 🛑

In the world of data engineering, "tracking changes" isn't a one-size-fits-all task. Depending on your goal—be it real-time streaming, efficient batch processing, or business auditing—you need a different tool in your kit.

Here is a quick breakdown of the "Big Three" change-tracking methods:

🔴 CDC (Change Data Capture)
The Vibe: "What just happened?"
How it works: It listens directly to the database transaction logs (think Kafka Connect).
Best for: Real-time synchronization, microservices, and reactive architectures where every millisecond counts.

🔵 CDF (Change Data Feed)
The Vibe: "What was written to the table?"
How it works: Specific to modern lakehouses (like Databricks/Delta Lake). It tracks version-to-version changes at the file level.
Best for: Simplifying ETL pipelines, incremental processing, and avoiding expensive "table diffs" in your data lake.

🟢 SCD Type 2 (Slowly Changing Dimension)
The Vibe: "What is the business history?"
How it works: It stores history by adding new rows with valid_from and valid_to timestamps.
Best for: Data warehousing and BI. If a user moves from NY to CA, you need to know which state to attribute their January sales to.

Which one should you choose?

Need real-time alerts? Use CDC.

Need to optimize your Lakehouse? Use CDF.

Need to report on historical trends? Use SCD Type 2.

The best architectures often use all three in tandem to move data from Source ➡️ Lake ➡️ Warehouse.

text:
Table vs View vs Materialized View

Understanding the difference between Table, View, and Materialized View is essential for designing scalable and high-performance data systems.

🔹 Table
A table is the base object in any database. It physically stores data on disk and acts as the single source of truth.

Stores actual data rows
Always up to date

Supports full DML operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)

Performance depends on size, partitioning, and indexing (or micro-partitioning in Snowflake)
Best suited for raw, staging, and curated datasets

🔹 View
A view is a virtual table created using a SELECT query. It does not store data, only the query definition.

No physical storage
Always reflects the latest data from base tables
Used for abstraction, security, and simplifying complex queries

Performance is similar to running the underlying query each time
Ideal for business logic, access control, and reusable query layers

🔹 Materialized View
A materialized view stores the pre-computed result of a query physically on disk.
Uses additional storage

Improves performance for heavy joins and aggregations

Data can become stale until refreshed
Higher maintenance compared to views
Best for frequently queried, expensive transformations

Boston Consulting Group (BCG) Data Engineer (X Delivery) | Interview Experience (Round 1, Round 2 & Round 3)

I recently appeared for the BCG Data Engineer (X Delivery) interview process and wanted to share my experience, as it may help others preparing for similar data engineering roles.

With 2 to 4 years of experience working across SQL, Python, PySpark, Databricks, and cloud-based data platforms, I found the overall process to be a strong test of real-world data engineering fundamentals, problem-solving I recently went through the interview process for the BCG Data Engineer (X Delivery) role and wanted to share my experience to help others preparing for similar positions.

✅ Round 1: Online Data Engineering Assessment
Advanced SQL (joins, NULLs, aggregations, CASE WHEN, optimized queries)
Python data engineering task (ingesting streaming data into SQLite, cursors, context managers)

✅ Round 2: Technical Interview (Fundamentals & Reasoning)
SQL execution order (WHERE vs GROUP BY vs HAVING)
Aliases in ORDER BY
Customer/order aggregations & January filtering
Palindrome-based string filtering
Translating SQL logic to PySpark

Python OOP concepts
Abstract base classes
Inheritance
Using super()
Abstract vs concrete methods
Perishable item with expiry-based 20% discount logic

✅ Round 3: Technical + Design Deep Dive
Advanced SQL & analytical thinking
PySpark transformations & window functions
Reusable Python classes & generic ingestion framework
Medallion (Bronze–Silver–Gold) architecture
Delta storage, schema standardization, data validation
Databricks Repos & CI/CD (DEV → QA → PROD)

After Round 3, the next step was expected to be a managerial + HR round, but it didn’t work out this time. Still, it was a valuable learning experience.

✅ Key Takeaways
Strong SQL fundamentals are essential
Be comfortable translating logic across SQL, Python, and PySpark
Debugging and reasoning matter as much as coding
Interviews test how you think, not just what you know
Sharing in case it helps others preparing for Data Engineer / Analytics Engineer / Big Data Engineer roles.

Happy to connect and exchange prep strategies 😊

text:
Data Engineering Interview Series – Part 6

A very common coding question in Data Engineering interviews is:

How do you find the top N records per group?

This is often asked to test your understanding of window functions and partitioning logic.

Use case: Find the top 2 highest-paid employees in each department.
Table: employee(emp_id, name, dept, salary)

Solution 1: Without using window functions

SELECT e1.*
FROM employee e1
WHERE (
 SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
 FROM employee e2
 WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept
 AND e2.salary > e1.salary
) < 2;

This is a correlated subquery approach and is often expected in theoretical discussions.

Solution 2: Using window functions (Preferred)

SELECT *
FROM (
 SELECT *,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (
 PARTITION BY dept
 ORDER BY salary DESC
 ) AS rnk
 FROM employee
) t
WHERE rnk <= 2;

This is the most common and scalable solution, and interviewers usually prefer this.

Solution 3: PySpark

from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import dense_rank, col

window_spec = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy(col("salary").desc())

df.withColumn("rnk", dense_rank().over(window_spec)) \
 .filter(col("rnk") <= 2)

This checks whether you understand partitioning and ranking in distributed systems.
